64.title: He washes their feet (John 13:1–17)
64.hook: the teacher kneels with a towel and washes twelve pairs of dusty feet
64.howItsDone: On Maundy Thursday, the Thursday before Easter, many Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches wash feet during the service. Some traditions, including many Brethren and Mennonite churches, practice foot washing regularly with communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jar of perfume, a year's wages poured out on his feet. Your line was love can be lavish. Did you give the compliment? Today, feet again, and this time he's the one kneeling. Day sixty-four.

Think of the jobs nobody wants. Cleaning the bathroom. Changing the diaper. Taking out the trash when it's leaking. There's always an unspoken question in a house about who does those. Now picture a room in Jerusalem, the night before Passover. Roads then were dust and dirt, and people walked them in sandals. When you arrived for dinner, a servant would wash your feet. It was one of the lowest jobs in the house. Tonight there's no servant. The disciples come in, and nobody picks up the basin. And then their teacher stands up from the table. Today, he washes their feet.
screen: `THE JOBS NOBODY WANTS.` → `DUSTY ROADS, OPEN SANDALS.` → `NOBODY PICKS UP THE BASIN.`

segments.voice: John opens the scene with one of the most tender lines in the Gospels, in the King James Bible: "having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Then Jesus gets up from supper, lays aside his outer clothes, and ties a towel around his waist, dressed like a servant. "After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded." He goes around the room. One pair of feet after another. Including the feet of Judas, who's about to betray him. Then he comes to Peter, and Peter can't bear it: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." And Peter, all or nothing as always, swings the other way: "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head." Afterward Jesus puts his clothes back on, sits down, and asks: do you know what I've done to you? You call me master and lord, and you're right. "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." I've given you an example. Later that night he gives them a new commandment: love one another, as I have loved you. In Latin, commandment is mandatum, and that's where the name Maundy Thursday comes from, the Thursday before Easter. On that day many churches still wash feet: the Pope does it, and so do many bishops, pastors and priests. Some churches, among the Brethren and Mennonites and others, practice foot washing regularly alongside communion. The one who ends up with a crown of thorns starts the night with a towel.
screen: `HE LOVED THEM UNTO THE END.` · `A TOWEL AROUND HIS WAIST.` · `PETER: NEVER MY FEET.` · `MANDATUM: MAUNDY THURSDAY.` · then, large: `YE ALSO OUGHT TO WASH ONE ANOTHER'S FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe slowly. Picture the basin going around the room, one pair of feet after another. Now think of one humble task waiting for you today. The dishes someone else left. The bin nobody takes out. The coffee pot. The shared bathroom. The email thread nobody wants to answer. Choose one. Plan to do it without saying anything. No announcement, no hint, no post. If anyone asks, just shrug. If you pray, you can offer it quietly. The bell holds the time.
He washes their feet. The teacher kneels with a towel and a basin, even at the feet of the one who will betray him.
Your line: the towel is the crown. Today, do one humble task without mentioning it, to anyone, ever. Day sixty-four.

what it means: the teacher takes a servant's lowest job, washes every pair of feet, including the betrayer's, and tells them to do the same.
what a scholar hears: mandatum, the new commandment of John 13:34, gave Maundy Thursday its name, and the towel, lention, is a Latin loanword for a servant's apron.

65.title: The last supper (Luke 22:14–20)
65.hook: bread broken, a cup shared, and "do this in remembrance of me"
65.howItsDone: Nearly all Christians share bread and wine, or grape juice, in memory of the Last Supper, called the Eucharist, Holy Communion, the Lord's Supper, the Mass or the Divine Liturgy. Some churches celebrate it every day or every Sunday, others monthly or a few times a year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he washes their feet, a teacher with a towel. Your line was the towel is the crown. What humble job did you do without a word? Today, the same night, the meal itself. Day sixty-five.

Think of a meal you'll never forget. Maybe the last dinner with someone before they moved away, or before they died. You didn't know it was the last one, or maybe you did. You remember where everyone sat. Now picture an upstairs room in Jerusalem. Passover, the feast when Jewish families remember how God brought their ancestors out of slavery in Egypt, with bread and wine and the old story told again. Jesus sits down with his friends. And he knows this is the last time. Today, the last supper.
screen: `A MEAL YOU'LL NEVER FORGET.` → `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM AT PASSOVER.` → `HE KNOWS IT'S THE LAST TIME.`

segments.voice: Luke gives us his first words at the table, in the King James Bible: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer." That doubling is a Hebrew way of saying, I have longed and longed for this. Then he does what the head of the table did at a Jewish meal. He takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and hands it around. But then he says something no one had heard at Passover before: "This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me." And after supper, the cup: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." Testament here means covenant, a binding promise between God and people, like the one made with Israel at Sinai. Now today's big word, remembrance. In Greek it's anamnesis. It means more than recalling a fact. At Passover, Jewish families speak as if they themselves came out of Egypt; the past becomes present at the table. Christians have done this meal ever since, and they understand it in different ways. Catholics and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood. Lutherans speak of Christ truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. Many Reformed Christians speak of a real spiritual presence. Many Baptists and others see it as a memorial, a powerful act of remembering. They call it different names too: the Eucharist, from the Greek for gave thanks; Holy Communion; the Lord's Supper; the Mass; the Divine Liturgy. What almost all of them share is the table, the bread, the cup, and his words: do this, and remember me.
screen: `WITH DESIRE I HAVE DESIRED.` · `BREAD TAKEN, BLESSED, BROKEN, GIVEN.` · `A NEW COVENANT IN A CUP.` · `ANAMNESIS: THE PAST MADE PRESENT.` · then, large: `THIS DO IN REMEMBRANCE OF ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and bring to mind the next meal you'll eat today. Picture it. Now think of someone you want to remember at that meal. Someone who's gone, or far away, or who taught you something at a table. What did they eat? What did they say? Where did they sit? Let them come close. Then plan to eat that meal slowly, no screen, a little quieter than usual, with them in mind. If you pray, you can give thanks before the first bite. The bell holds the time.
The last supper. Bread broken, a cup shared, on the night before he died, and the words Christians repeat at the table to this day: do this in remembrance of me.
Your line: remember me. Today, eat one meal slowly, remembering someone who once sat at your table. Day sixty-five.

what it means: a Passover meal where he gives bread and a cup new meaning, and asks his friends to do it again, remembering him.
what a scholar hears: anamnesis, remembrance, echoes Passover's way of making the past present, and Luke alone mentions a cup before the bread as well as after.

66.title: Gethsemane (Luke 22:39–46)
66.hook: in a garden at night he prays, sweating, not my will but yours
66.howItsDone: Many churches keep a watch on the night of Maundy Thursday, staying up to pray in memory of Gethsemane, and some Christians keep a holy hour of prayer on other nights. Pilgrims to Jerusalem visit an olive garden on the Mount of Olives with very old trees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last supper, bread and a cup, and your line: remember me. Who did you remember at the table? After the meal, they sing, and walk out into the dark. Day sixty-six.

Think of the worst night you've had before something you dreaded. The night before surgery. The night before a hard goodbye. Lying awake, bargaining with the ceiling. Now picture a hillside across a small valley from Jerusalem, the Mount of Olives, late at night. Jesus goes there, Luke says, as he often did, and his disciples follow. Matthew and Mark name the place: Gethsemane. It was an olive grove, and the name probably means oil press, the place where olives are crushed. Tonight he's the one being pressed. Today's word: Gethsemane.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DREADED THING.` → `THE MOUNT OF OLIVES, LATE.` → `GETHSEMANE: THE OIL PRESS.`

segments.voice: He tells his friends to pray that they don't fall into testing. Then he goes a stone's throw away, kneels, and prays, in the King James Bible: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Notice what he asks first. Take it away. He doesn't pretend he wants to suffer. He asks, honestly, for another way. The cup, in the prophets, is often a picture of suffering. And only then: nevertheless. That word again, the one Peter said on the lake. Not my will, but yours. In Mark he calls God Abba, the family word for father. Then Luke gives a detail that's stayed with readers for centuries: "And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground." As it were. Like drops of blood. Luke may mean his sweat fell heavy as blood, or that it was mixed with blood; readers have taken it both ways. And a small honesty: these verses, and the angel who comes to strengthen him, are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts of Luke, though many others have them. Agony, in Greek agonia, was the word for the strain of a wrestler or a runner at the end of a race. And his friends? He comes back and finds them asleep, Luke says, sleeping for sorrow. He wakes them gently: "Why sleep ye? rise and pray, lest ye enter into temptation." This is the prayer many Christians find the most honest in the Bible: say what you want, say it fully, and then let go.
screen: `REMOVE THIS CUP FROM ME.` · `NEVERTHELESS, NOT MY WILL.` · `AGONIA: A WRESTLER'S STRAIN.` · `SLEEPING FOR SORROW.` · then, large: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE, BE DONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let yourself get still. Think of the hardest thing in front of you right now. Something you'd take away if you could. Don't dress it up. In your own words, silently, say what you really want. All of it. Take it away, or make it different, or let me off. Then, if you can, notice what it would be like to hold it a little more loosely. You don't have to get to nevertheless today. If you pray, you can pray it to God just as honestly. The bell holds the time.
Gethsemane. An olive grove whose name probably means oil press, where he prayed take this cup away, and then, not my will.
Your line: not my will. Today, when something doesn't go your way, say what you wanted honestly first, then see if you can loosen your grip, even a little. Day sixty-six.

67.title: The rooster crows (Luke 22:54–62)
67.hook: Peter swears three times he never knew him, then the rooster, then the look
67.howItsDone: Peter's denial is read in Holy Week in many churches, and it's sung in the Passion settings of Bach and others. Weathervanes shaped like roosters sit on many church steeples, especially in Europe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gethsemane: take this cup, and then, not my will. Your line was not my will. Where did you loosen your grip? That same night, soldiers come to the garden. Day sixty-seven.

Think of a time you said something you swore you'd never say. You pretended you didn't know someone. You laughed along. You kept quiet when you should have spoken. Most of us have a moment like that. Now picture a courtyard in Jerusalem in the middle of the night. Jesus has been arrested and taken into the high priest's house. Most of his friends have scattered. But Peter, Peter who walked on water, Peter who said he'd go to prison and to death with him, follows at a distance. He slips into the courtyard and sits down by a fire with the servants and guards, warming his hands. Today, the rooster crows.
screen: `THE THING YOU SWORE YOU'D NEVER SAY.` → `ARRESTED IN THE NIGHT.` → `PETER BY THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: A servant girl looks at him in the firelight and says: this man was with him. And Peter, in the King James Bible: "Woman, I know him not." A little later someone else: you're one of them. "Man, I am not." About an hour later, a third person insists: surely this fellow was with him, he's a Galilean, you can hear it in his accent. And Peter says: "Man, I know not what thou sayest." And while he's still speaking, the rooster crows. Earlier that evening Jesus had told him exactly this, and Peter had said never. Then Luke adds a detail no other Gospel has: "And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter." Across the courtyard, their eyes meet. Luke doesn't describe the look. Angry? Sad? Loving? The sources are silent, and readers have wondered ever since. "And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And Peter went out, and wept bitterly." Here's what's remarkable. This story is in all four Gospels. The early church could have hidden the moment its most famous leader failed. Instead they told it everywhere. Peter, the rock, the one with the keys, is also the one who said three times, I don't know him. Christians have found courage in that for two thousand years. Failure isn't the end of Peter's story. The rooster became a symbol of it, and you'll still see a rooster on top of many church steeples, a reminder to stay awake, and that even Peter fell, and was not finished.
screen: `WOMAN, I KNOW HIM NOT.` · `THREE TIMES, THEN THE ROOSTER.` · `THE LORD TURNED AND LOOKED.` · `TOLD IN ALL FOUR GOSPELS.` · then, large: `PETER WENT OUT, AND WEPT BITTERLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind one old failure you still carry. A time you let someone down, or yourself. Not to replay it. Just to look at it once, honestly. Now notice how long you've been carrying it. Think of Peter weeping in the dark, and remember that his story didn't end there. Try saying to yourself, quietly: that happened, and I'm more than that. If you pray, you can ask to be forgiven and to forgive yourself. The bell holds the time.
The rooster crows. Three denials by a fire, a rooster, a look across the courtyard, and a man weeping bitterly, who wasn't finished.
Your line: even peter. Today, when you remember the old failure, let it be a story that goes on, not one that ends there. Day sixty-seven.

68.title: Pilate and Simon (Luke 23:13–26)
68.hook: a governor washes his hands; a passer-by from Cyrene is made to carry the cross
68.tomorrow: At the foot of the cross
68.howItsDone: Many Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches pray the Stations of the Cross in Lent, walking or meditating on fourteen moments of Jesus's last journey; Simon of Cyrene helping to carry the cross is the fifth. Christians often recite in the creeds that he suffered under Pontius Pilate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rooster crows, and Peter weeps by the fire. Your line was even peter. What old failure did you set down? Now it's morning, and two very different men step into the story. Day sixty-eight.

Think about the difference between the person with the power to stop something and the person who just happens to be walking by. One can make a decision. The other can only help carry it. Now picture Jerusalem at dawn. After a night of questioning, Jesus is brought to the Roman governor of Judea, Pontius Pilate. Only Rome could order a crucifixion, and crucifixion was Rome's punishment for rebels and slaves. Pilate holds all the power in this scene. And somewhere outside the city, a man from North Africa is walking in from the countryside, with no idea what's about to happen to him. Today, Pilate and Simon.
screen: `THE ONE WITH POWER, THE ONE PASSING BY.` → `PONTIUS PILATE, AT DAWN.` → `ONLY ROME COULD CRUCIFY.`

segments.voice: Pilate questions Jesus and says to the chief priests and the crowd, in the King James Bible: "I find no fault in this man." He says it again. In Luke he says it three times. He sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, who mocks him and sends him back. Pilate offers to have him whipped and let go. But the people gathered in the courtyard shout for Barabbas, a man in prison for rebellion and murder, and they cry out: "Crucify him, crucify him." And Pilate, who has the power, gives in. He releases Barabbas and hands Jesus over to be crucified. The famous hand-washing isn't in Luke; it's in Matthew, where Pilate washes his hands before the crowd and says: "I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it." But water doesn't wash away a decision. It was Pilate's order and Roman soldiers who carried it out, and for centuries some Christians wrongly blamed the Jewish people as a whole. Many churches have since rejected that blame plainly. Then Luke turns to the other man: "And as they led him away, they laid hold upon one Simon, a Cyrenian, coming out of the country, and on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus." Cyrene was a city in North Africa, in what is now Libya, with a large Jewish community. Simon was probably a pilgrim in town for Passover. He didn't volunteer. Soldiers could force anyone to carry a load. But Mark names his sons, Alexander and Rufus, as if the first readers knew them. It seems the man forced to carry the cross became part of the story himself.
screen: `I FIND NO FAULT IN THIS MAN.` · `CRUCIFY HIM, CRUCIFY HIM.` · `WATER DOESN'T WASH A DECISION.` · `SIMON OF CYRENE, FROM THE COUNTRY.` · then, large: `THAT HE MIGHT BEAR IT AFTER JESUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think of someone near you who's carrying something heavy right now. A diagnosis. A caregiving load. A lost job. A child in trouble. Grief. You can't take it away. Neither could Simon. But he could carry part of it for a while. Picture one practical piece of their load you could carry today. A meal. A ride. An errand. A few hours of company. Pick one. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Pilate and Simon. The governor who had the power to stop it and didn't, and the passer-by from Cyrene who was made to carry the cross.
Your line: someone carried it with him. Today, carry one practical thing for someone who's weighed down. Day sixty-eight.

69.title: At the foot of the cross (John 19:25–30)
69.word: At the foot of the cross
69.hook: his mother stands there, and he gives her and John to each other
69.howItsDone: On Good Friday, many churches read the Passion from John's Gospel, and some hold three hours of prayer and silence in the afternoon. The Stabat Mater is sung in many churches, and Catholics and others remember Our Lady of Sorrows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pilate and Simon: the man with the power, and the man who carried the cross. Your line was someone carried it with him. What did you carry? Today, the hardest place in the story. Day sixty-nine.

If you've ever sat by a hospital bed, you know there comes a point where there's nothing left to do. No more phone calls, no more questions for the doctor. Just being there. Staying. Now picture a hill outside Jerusalem called Golgotha, and a Roman cross. Most of Jesus's friends have run. But John says a small group is standing near the cross. It was dangerous to be seen with a man Rome was executing as a rebel. They stayed anyway. Today, at the foot of the cross.
screen: `BY A HOSPITAL BED.` → `GOLGOTHA, OUTSIDE THE CITY.` → `A FEW WHO STAYED.`

segments.voice: John names them, in the King James Bible: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene." Mostly women. And one man John never names, only calls the disciple whom Jesus loved; Christian tradition has long said this was John himself. Think of Mary, his mother. The one who said let it be to the angel, who wrapped him in cloths and laid him in a manger, who heard Simeon say a sword would pierce her own soul. Now she's here. Then Jesus, in terrible pain, looks down and takes care of her. "Woman, behold thy son!" And to the disciple: "Behold thy mother!" And John says: "And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home." Even on the cross he's making sure his mother won't be alone. Many Christians read more here too: Catholics and Orthodox Christians often see Mary given as a mother to every disciple. Then he says: "I thirst." They lift a sponge of sour wine to his mouth. And then three words in English, one word in Greek: "It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost." The Greek is tetelestai. It means finished, completed, accomplished, brought to its end. Not I'm finished, as in defeated. It is finished, as in done, the work completed. For many centuries Christians have sung a Latin hymn about this scene called Stabat Mater, the mother was standing. Because that's what she did. She couldn't stop it. She couldn't fix it. She stood there. She stayed.
screen: `THERE STOOD BY THE CROSS HIS MOTHER.` · `WOMAN, BEHOLD THY SON.` · `I THIRST.` · `TETELESTAI: COMPLETED.` · then, large: `IT IS FINISHED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let yourself be still. Think of someone who is suffering right now. Someone sick, grieving, lonely, stuck, or just worn down. You probably can't fix it. That's hard. Instead of looking for the fix, picture simply being with them. Sitting in the room. Staying on the phone a little longer. Not leaving when it gets uncomfortable. Hold them in mind for the rest of the sit, and just stay. If you pray, you can hold them before God without words. The bell holds the time.
At the foot of the cross. A mother, a few women, and one beloved disciple who stayed, and the last word: tetelestai, it is finished.
screen: `AT THE FOOT OF THE CROSS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: stay. Today, stay with someone who is suffering, in person, by phone, or by message, a little longer than is comfortable. Day sixty-nine.

what a scholar hears: tetelestai is a perfect-tense verb, a thing completed with lasting effect, and the beloved disciple is never named in John's Gospel.

70.title: Mary Magdalene in the garden (John 20:11–18)
70.hook: weeping, she mistakes him for the gardener until he says her name
70.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the resurrection at Easter, the most important feast of the Christian year, often with a vigil or a sunrise service. The Catholic Church keeps Mary Magdalene's feast on July 22, calling her the apostle to the apostles, and Orthodox Christians honor her as equal to the apostles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at the foot of the cross, a few who stayed, and your line: stay. Who did you stay with? He was buried in a garden tomb before the Sabbath. Now it's the first day of the week, early, still dark. Day seventy, and the end of week ten.

Grief makes you do strange things. You drive past their house. You keep their voicemail. You go back to the place, because it's the last place they were. Mary Magdalene goes to the tomb while it's still dark. She was one of the women who traveled with Jesus and supported him; Luke says he had freed her from seven demons. She stood at the cross. And now she finds the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. She runs for Peter and the beloved disciple; they come, look, and go home. But Mary stays outside the tomb, weeping. Today, Mary Magdalene in the garden.
screen: `GRIEF MAKES YOU GO BACK.` → `THE STONE ROLLED AWAY.` → `MARY STAYS, WEEPING.`

segments.voice: She stoops to look in, and sees two angels in white, sitting where his body had been. They ask why she's weeping, and she says, in the King James Bible: "Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him." She turns around, and someone is standing there. "Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou?" She thinks he's the gardener: "Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away." She doesn't recognize him. Her eyes are full of tears, and the dead don't stand in gardens. Then one word: "Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master." That's the moment. Not a sermon. Not a proof. Her name, said the way only he said it. Rabboni means my teacher, and it's a word of closeness. Then he tells her not to cling to him, and sends her to tell the others, and she goes and says: "I have seen the Lord." This is the heart of Christian faith: that Jesus rose from the dead. And in John the first person to see him, and the first sent to tell it, is a woman who stayed when the others went home. Early Christian writers called her the apostle to the apostles. And one myth to clear away: the Bible never says she was a prostitute. That idea came from a sermon centuries later that mixed her up with other women in the Gospels. This week began with a towel and a basin. Then the last supper, Gethsemane, the rooster, Pilate and Simon, the cross. Now a garden, and a name.
screen: `THEY HAVE TAKEN AWAY MY LORD.` · `SHE THINKS HE'S THE GARDENER.` · `MARY. RABBONI.` · `THE APOSTLE TO THE APOSTLES.` · then, large: `I HAVE SEEN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of someone who says your name kindly. A grandparent, a friend, a teacher, a partner, someone who's gone. Hear it the way they say it. Notice what happens in your chest when you do. Mary knew him the moment he said her name. Now, in the quiet, let your own name be said kindly, as if by someone who knows you completely and isn't disappointed. If you pray, you can listen for it from God. The bell holds the time.

Mary Magdalene in the garden. The first to see him risen in John's Gospel, and the first sent to tell it. These two weeks' words: the keys, transfiguration, Lazarus, hosanna, the last supper, Gethsemane.
